match.reason: The closest bank point, The bill of rights debate, is about whether courts or parliaments should protect rights, not about how far a particular right should extend or how it should be balanced against others, so it teaches a related but different idea.

draft.title: Conflicting attitudes to a right
card: People and groups often agree that a right matters but disagree on how far it should go. Their attitudes come from their values, experiences and interests.
Rights can clash with each other. Freedom of expression can clash with a person's right to a good reputation, or with the right to be free from discrimination.
Rights can also clash with the wider interests of the community, such as safety and public order. Lawmakers must decide where to draw the line.
Because of this, most rights are not absolute. A right can be limited by law where the limit is reasonable, and different groups may argue that the limit is too wide or too narrow.
draft.remember: People agree a right matters but disagree on its limits, because rights are balanced against other rights and community interests.

a.q: Two groups both support freedom of expression. One wants limits on hateful speech and the other wants none. What does this show?
opts: They disagree on how far the right should go
They disagree that the right exists at all
They have no values behind their attitudes
The right must be absolute for one of them
a.why: Both groups accept the right. They differ on its limits, which is a conflict of attitudes about how far it should go. The option about not accepting the right is wrong because both groups support it.
a.clue: Do both groups accept the right itself?

b.q: A council bans protests near a hospital entrance so patients can get in. Organiser Priya says the ban is too wide. What is the main conflict here?
opts: Freedom of assembly against patient access and safety
Freedom of assembly against the right to vote
Two groups who both want the ban removed
A dispute over whether any rights exist
b.why: The council is balancing the right to protest against patients' access and safety, which are community interests. Priya's view is that the balance is wrong, not that the right does not exist. The voting option has nothing to do with the case.
b.clue: What is the council protecting by limiting the protest?

a.best: They disagree on how far the right should go

b.best: Freedom of assembly against patient access and safety

problems.detail: The distractor 'The right must be absolute for one of them' uses 'must', while the card says rights 'can' be limited. It is also arguable: the group that wants no limits does treat the right as absolute, so a careful student could defend this option.

The right option, 'Freedom of assembly against patient access and safety', is the longest and most specific. It also matches the clue about what the council is protecting, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

a.q: Two groups both support freedom of expression. One wants limits on hateful speech and the other wants none. What does this show?
opts: They disagree on how far the right should go
They disagree that the right exists at all
They share the same view of the right's limits
Their attitudes have no basis in their values

b.q: A council bans protest marches on a main highway at peak hour to stop crashes and traffic chaos. Organiser Priya says the ban is too wide. What clash is this?
opts: A right weighed against safety and public order
A right weighed against another person's right
A dispute over whether the right should exist
A dispute over whether the right has any limits
b.why: The council limits the right to protest to protect safety and public order, which are interests of the wider community. No other person's right, such as reputation, is at stake. Priya accepts some limit but says this one is too wide, so she is not denying the right or all limits.
b.clue: Look at the reason the council gives for its ban.

b.best: A right weighed against safety and public order
